lesson.title: The Raw Material of Every Statistical Question
lesson.summary: This section defines data as recorded facts or measurements, distinguishes data from the real world phenomena it represents, and introduces the classroom quiz score dataset used throughout later sections.
lesson.body:
In the previous section, statistics was defined as the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, and interpreting information. That information itself has a name: data. Data is the collection of facts, measurements, or observations that have been recorded, usually because someone wanted to answer a question with them. A single temperature reading, a single yes or no survey answer, a single price tag, these are all pieces of data. Data does not have to be numeric. A list of favorite colors or a list of countries visited is still data, just not the kind you can average.

It is worth pausing on the difference between the real world and data about the real world. A student's actual height is a physical fact that exists whether or not anyone measures it. The number 63 inches, written down in a teacher's notebook after using a tape measure, is data: a recorded representation of that fact. This distinction matters because recording always introduces some possibility of error or loss. A measurement can be read incorrectly, a survey respondent can misunderstand a question, a sensor can malfunction. Part of doing statistics responsibly is remembering that data is a stand in for reality, not reality itself, and thinking critically about how well that stand in actually represents what you care about.

Data is typically gathered for a reason: to answer a specific question. A teacher who wants to know how a class performed on a quiz needs data on quiz scores. A city that wants to know whether a new stoplight reduced accidents needs data on accident counts before and after installation. The question you are trying to answer should guide exactly what data you collect. Collecting data without a clear question in mind often results in a pile of numbers that cannot actually answer anything useful.

Consider a small worked example that will be reused throughout the next several sections. A teacher records information about 8 students in a class: their quiz score out of 10 points, and their height in inches. The eight recorded quiz scores are 7, 8, 6, 9, 7, 5, 8, and 10. That list of eight numbers is data. Even before doing anything sophisticated, we can summarize it: adding all eight scores gives 7 + 8 + 6 + 9 + 7 + 5 + 8 + 10 = 60, and dividing by the 8 students gives an average score of 60 divided by 8, which equals 7.5. That average, 7.5, was computed directly from the recorded data, and it would be meaningless without it. No data, no average, no statistics.

Once you have data in hand, the next step is figuring out how to describe its structure. The next few sections build directly on this idea of data: a variable describes what kind of information was recorded for each student, an observation describes the information recorded about one particular student, and a dataset describes the full table that results when many observations of many variables are collected and organized together.
